#3336. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3335. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

#3334. Halide camera app just got even better for iPhone Duo

Halide 3.4 is out today as the latest update to the pro camera app. The update adds several new features, including a larger viewfinder for iPhone Duo and more.

The new Halide update also lets you use the outer screen on iPhone Duo as a live preview or a fill flash. It brings back a few camera tools from Halide Mark II as well.

Lux Optics first added iPhone Duo support in October with Halide 3.3. With the phone fully open, the initial iPhone Duo update let you review your most recent photo alongside the live viewfinder.

Today’s new XL mode gives you the option to swap the photo preview for a larger viewfinder. Controls on both sides enable two-handed shooting.

While the Duo is open, the outer screen can mirror Halide’s camera controls or show a full-screen viewfinder without controls. The second option lets the person you’re photographing see how you’ve framed the shot.

In low light, Halide can use the outer screen as a fill flash. That gives you a softer source of light for portraits, and Halide’s developers recommend turning the screen brightness all the way up before taking the photo.

Halide also now places the histogram along the Duo’s crease. The update revises the Photo Lab interface for editing with the Duo half open as well.

On other iPhones, Halide 3.4 restores the color and luminance histograms and the shutter timer from Mark II.

Halide Mark III launched back in May with a redesigned camera and the new Photo Lab editor. Recent updates added RAW-only capture in 3.1 and Aperture Priority for iPhone 18 Pro in 3.2. Halide Mark III version 3.4 is available now on the App Store.

#3332. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale."

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3329. iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a convenient new setting, here’s how to use it

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of new features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

New in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

You can also move the new slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

Mark Gurman reports that Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to replace McCormack, who reported to software chief Craig Federighi. “Instead, his former deputies are assuming his responsibilities under other executives,” the report says.

In his role, McCormack oversaw “close coordination between software engineers and Apple’s camera hardware and chip teams.” He’s credited with last year’s redesigned selfie camera and other projects:

His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 lineup last year. This year, Apple added a variable-aperture camera to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, giving users more control over lighting and depth of field. Bloomberg describes McCormack as a “strong opponent of using generative AI to create or alter photographs,” a philosophy that created tension as Apple embraced AI tools in the Photos app. His retirement, however, “wasn’t related to a disagreement or clash with Apple over its AI strategy,” the report says.

#3323. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

#3322. Gemini app for Mac adds computer use to control desktop apps

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#3320. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

#3318. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 stocks for the long haul

Global stock markets have been volatile as investors assess high bond yields and continued tensions between the U.S. and Iran. There are concerns about the impact of uncertainty in the Middle East on oil prices and consequently on inflation.

Investors who prefer to look beyond short-term noise and buy stocks with attractive long-term growth potential can follow the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. The ratings of these experts are backed by in-depth research of a company's financials and thorough analysis of the factors affecting its business performance.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Semiconductor giant Nvidia (NVDA) reported stellar fiscal second-quarter results and reassured investors about continued strength in AI-driven demand for its chips. Moreover, Nvidia's FY28 revenue growth outlook of 70% was well above the Street's expectations.

Reacting to the Q2 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reiterated a buy rating on NVDA and increased his price target to $300 from $288. "This is our Top Pick in the semis group, with a compelling product cycle, exceptional growth and valuation below peers," said the 5-star analyst.

Nvidia delivered impressive quarterly results despite supply constraints, Moore said, but he believes that the FY28 revenue and gross margin commentary mattered more, with a favorable outlook for both measures.

Moore said Nvidia's 70% revenue growth guidance for FY28 was above his own estimate of 52% and the consensus of about 40%. The top-line growth estimate was a "remarkable figure" given supply issues and Moore said he expects Nvidia to continue to address bottlenecks to deliver rapid growth.

Among other takeaways, the analyst said performance metrics for Vera Rubin chips were strong, with Nvidia emphasizing a 30x higher throughput per megawatt and 35x lower token cost compared with Grace Blackwell Ultra.

Moore ranks No. 159 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 24.60%. See Nvidia Statistics on TipRanks.

Ride-hailing and delivery platform Uber Technologies (UBER) was recommended by BMO Capital analyst Brian Pitz, who discussed the company's opportunity in the autonomous vehicle (AV) market in a recent research note that reiterated a buy rating and price target of $119.

The 5-star analyst highlighted Uber's transition into a diversified marketplace, with investors now focusing on its AV growth prospects. The key question is how much value can Uber generate as AVs become commercialized, Pitz asked.

"We continue to believe that Uber's AV strategy is evolving and will become a significant driver of revenue and profitability," the analyst said.

Importantly, Pitz believes that Uber can establish itself as a preferred mobility platform for AV makers, supported by its growing AV infrastructure capabilities and an expanding partner base. This would enable Uber to win a significant share of value as the AV market is commercialized.

Additionally, Pitz noted Uber's enhanced position in the AV value chain, with the company shifting from serving as a distribution channel for robotaxis to becoming a broader platform for AV mobility. The analyst discussed Uber's efforts to capture growth opportunities in the AV market, including higher capital spending, expansion into new markets and building partnerships beyond Alphabet's Waymo.

Pitz ranks No. 574 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of about 12.20%. See Uber Technologies Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the second quarter of FY27. But the company's increased FY28 guidance fell short of investors' high expectations.

In reaction to the Q2 FY27 results, KeyBanc analyst John Vinh reaffirmed a buy rating on Marvell Technology, with a price target of $400. The analyst noted that Marvell's results and outlook were driven by strength in its data center business. The Q2 FY27 data center business grew 46% year-over-year, to $2.17 billion, far above KeyBanc's estimate of $2.09 billion.

Management "highlighted accelerating AI networking demand across scale-out, scale-across and scale-up architectures, supported by strong 800G optical DSP demand, rapid 1.6T ramp, broader 51.2T switch deployments and higher TIA/driver demand," Vinh said.

Consequently, Marvell raised its data center revenue guidance, now expecting 60% growth in FY27 and more than 60% in FY28.

Regarding the recently announced $120 billion warrant arrangement with Google, Vinh said management argued that programs tied to the warrant are already priced into the custom outlook through FY28. Meanwhile, new programs and those in execution are expected to drive significant upside to the previous FY29 custom XPU revenue estimate of over $10 billion, Vinh said, citing management.

Vinh ranks No. 123 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 28.50%. See Marvell Technology Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

#3316. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3315. I’m a Deals Writer, and These Are My Top 10 Tech Deals This Week

As Lifehacker's deals writer, I'm always looking for the best bargains on TVs, speakers, laptops, and other tech. Now that it's Friday, I've rounded up this week's sales highlights.

This week, you can already feel the early Black Friday deals heating up with the sale starting next week. Amazon has many tech deals, as do Costco, Walmart, and other retailers. You can find price cuts on the M5 MacBook Air, the best headphones of 2026, Kindle readers, and more.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 are one of the best premium headphones of 2026, and right now, Amazon is offering them with a 24% on them right now. That brings the price of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones down to $348. You're not likely to see these headphones drop any further in price anytime soon, even with Black Friday coming up. So if you've had your eyes on the XM6, this is likely the best deal you'll get for a while.

The Kindle Paperwhite is having one of its best discounts right now, dropping to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors. This is the classic, standard e-reader from Amazon, but since it's not the Signature Edition, you'll have to put up with ads and the minimum 16GB storage (which still gets you storage for over a thousand e-books). There are other e-readers on sale as well if you want to see other options.

The MacBook Air with the M5 chip comes in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $250 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,049.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,249 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case.

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269). This is a great opportunity to snatch a quality portable speaker with a big discount.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $19.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade.

The Sony WH-CH730N are $98 (originally $179), the lowest price they've ever been. They use the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0.

Samsung’s HW-Q600F soundbar is down to $379.99 at Amazon from $499.99, a $120 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever. This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup. Dolby Atmos also brings a modest sense of height, and effects track cleanly from left to right. You get a graphic equalizer and sound presets for adjusting the audio to your preferences through the included remote.

The Ultimate Ears Miniroll is down to $49.99 (originally $79.99), the second-lowest it has sold for so far. It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. I still haven't started my holiday shopping, but that's OK — I have plenty of movies to watch! As November stretches on, I need a great movie night now more than ever. Good thing Prime Video has loaded up its ever-tempting library this month, so rather than letting you burn half the evening scrolling, I’ve picked out three films I reckon will see you through the weekend in style on one of the best streaming services out there.

First up is a brand-new biopic that turns Nicolas Cage loose as John Madden, and he's weirdly perfect in the role. Then there’s a gloriously daft comic-book romp that bombed back in 1995 and has spent the decades building a devoted cult. And to round things off, I’ve gone for a cheesy, heartwarming Disney holiday comedy from peak Jonathan Taylor Thomas.

So cozy up with your blanket, raid the fridge for some snacks, and read on for three movies worth streaming on Prime Video this weekend.

I didn’t have “Nicolas Cage plays John Madden” on my 2026 bingo card, but here we are, and I’m thrilled about it, even though I don't much care for football. I care about games, and I care about Cage, and you get plenty of both here.

“Madden” is a biopic of the Hall of Fame coach, broadcaster and game namesake, and Cage throws himself into the role with exactly the kind of energy you're probably hoping for. Director David O. Russell traces Madden’s whole arc, from his Super Bowl-winning years running the Oakland Raiders to the legendary broadcasting career that made him a household name, right up to the video game that slapped his name on millions of games for multiple consoles.

Whether you grew up quoting Madden’s broadcasts or just spent your weekends button-mashing through “Madden NFL,” this one’s a loving, larger-than-life tribute to an American original.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

If your nostalgia receptors are still calibrated to the late ’90s, “I’ll Be Home for Christmas” is going to hit you like a Mack truck. This 1998 Disney comedy is pure, uncut comfort food, starring peak-era Jonathan Taylor Thomas. He plays Jake, a spoiled college kid on the west coast whose estranged dad (Gary Cole) dangles a vintage Porsche in front of him if he can just make it home to New York for Christmas.

Naturally, nothing goes as it should. Some classmates strand Jake out in the desert wearing a Santa suit and beard, and he has to figure out how to get home before the holiday clock runs out. Meanwhile, his girlfriend Allie (Jessica Biel) gives up waiting and accepts a cross-country ride from Jake’s rival.

Look, it’s not reinventing the genre, and that's fine. But JTT is genuinely charming as a selfish kid who slowly figures out what the season’s actually about. Relax and let the holiday vibes wash over you.

Watch "I'll Be Home For Christmas" on Prime Video

Some movies are good, some movies are bad, and some movies are “Tank Girl." This 1995 cult oddity flopped on release and then spent the next three decades becoming the kind of movie people force their friends to watch at 1 a.m. I am now one of those people, so consider this me pressing it on you.

Lori Petty is Rebecca Buck, aka Tank Girl, a punky blonde surviving in a post-apocalyptic 2033 where a nasty megacorporation called Water & Power is hoarding all the well, water and power. When Kesslee (Malcolm McDowell) kills her friends and burns down her life, Rebecca commandeers a tank, teams up Jet Girl (Naomi Watts) and a band of kangaroo-human mutant rebels called the Rippers, and sets out to bring the whole system down.

Adapted from the Jamie Hewlett and Alan Martin comic, years before Hewlett co-created Gorillaz, the movie is an explosion of punk attitude, comic-book panels, musical numbers, and anything-goes weirdness. It makes almost no sense and absolutely does not care, and that's absolutely why you should check it out. Yesterday.

#3312. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3311. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface.
